title: Use the substitution x = a sin^2(θ) to integrate expressions of the form sqrt(x(a-x))
content: When you need to integrate sqrt(x(a-x)) (equivalently x^(1/2)(a-x)^(1/2)) between limits 0 and a, where a is a positive constant, substitute x = a sin^2(θ). This works because a - x = a(1 - sin^2θ) = a cos^2θ, so sqrt(x(a-x)) = sqrt(a sin^2θ · a cos^2θ) = a sinθ cosθ, which pairs neatly with dx = 2a sinθ cosθ dθ to give an integrand proportional to sin^2θ cos^2θ (i.e. proportional to sin^2(2θ) once you use sin(2θ) = 2sinθ cosθ). Convert the limits too: x = 0 gives θ = 0, and x = a gives θ = π/2 (since sin^2θ = 1 there). Once you have an integral in sin^2(2θ), use the double angle identity sin^2(2θ) = (1 - cos4θ)/2 to make it directly integrable, then substitute the θ-limits. This is the standard trick whenever you meet the square root of a quadratic that factorises as x(a-x) - i.e. an 'upside-down' quadratic with roots at 0 and a.
